t1_mistake_agree.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.m_y: Agree is a verb, so you don't need am.
script.m_x: I agree. I don't agree. Do you agree?
script.m_t: To agree strongly, say: I totally agree.
script.m_q: Quiz! Which one is right, A or B?
script.m_c: Check your grammar free on lexkite.com.

t1_mistake_agree.note: “I am agree” is a very common learner error (agree is a verb, not an adjective). “I agree.” / “I don't agree.” / “Do you agree?” are standard US English. Quiz answer B is right. “I totally agree” is a natural US intensifier.

t2_words5_hotel.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.w_1: One: key. Can I get a second key?
script.w_2: Two: luggage. Can you hold my luggage?
script.w_4: Four: shower. The shower isn't working.
script.w_5: Five: receipt. The p is silent.
script.w_6: Can I get a receipt, please?
script.w_r: Which word was new for you?
script.w_t: Save this for your next trip!
script.w_c: Review these words free on lexkite.com.

t2_words5_hotel.note: Five hotel nouns, each with a natural US example: second key, hold my luggage (uncountable), elevator (US), the shower isn't working, can I get a receipt (silent p — true: /rɪˈsiːt/).

t3_guess_elevator.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.g_c: Hint: it takes you up and down.
script.g_u: In British English, it's a lift.
script.g_v: But in America, we say elevator.
script.g_x: Try it: Excuse me, where's the elevator?
script.g_s: Look up any word free on lexkite.com.

t3_guess_elevator.note: Picture clue = elevator icon, hint “takes you up and down” fits, answer revealed after 3-2-1. UK “lift” vs US “elevator” is accurate. “Excuse me, where's the elevator?” is the natural US question.

t4_pair_borrow_lend.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.p_h: Borrow or lend? Don't mix them up.
script.p_b: Borrow means you take it, then give it back.
script.p_l: Lend means you give it, and get it back.
script.p_l2: Can you lend me your pen?
script.p_q: Quiz! My brother blank me ten dollars.
script.p_a: Lent! My brother lent me ten dollars.
script.p_c: Compare tricky words free on lexkite.com.

t4_pair_borrow_lend.note: Borrow = take (and return), lend = give (and get back). “Can I borrow your pen?” / “Can you lend me your pen?” standard. Quiz: “My brother lent me ten dollars” correct; “borrowed me” is non-standard.

t5_roleplay_checkin.hook: ✈️ AIRPORT CHECK-IN / What do you say?
t5_roleplay_checkin.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.r_h: Airport check-in. Here's what to say.
script.r_1: Hi! Can I see your passport, please?
script.r_3: Are you checking any bags today?
script.r_5: Your turn. Ask for a window seat.
script.r_6: Could I get a window seat, please?

t5_roleplay_checkin.note: Natural US airport check-in exchange (agent: passport, checking bags; traveler: here you go, just one). Your-turn prompt + model answer “Could I get a window seat, please?” is polite and idiomatic.

t6_pron_comfortable.reviewer: Claude (expert American English teacher review, 25/10/2026; no GrabCast)

script.f_h: Many learners say this word wrong.
script.f_r: Most Americans say three beats. Stress the first one.
script.f_y: Your turn. Repeat after me: comfortable.

t6_pron_comfortable.note: comfortable /ˈkʌmftərbəl/: US dictionaries list the 3-syllable KUMF-ter-bul first; stress on the first syllable. Stressing “TA” (com-for-TA-ble) is a typical learner error. Slow (TTS 0.7) then normal speed, then repeat-after-me pause.
